title: Fill in the Blanks
summary: One sentence, one or two blanks, four options — decided almost always by a collocation, a phrasal unit, a tense anchor or a confusable pair, not by dictionary size. Every blank has a governor (a word beside it) that dictates the answer; finding that governor first is the whole technique.

subtopics.title: Collocation blanks: word partnerships that decide the answer
subtopics.concept:
A collocation is a pair of words that native usage glues together. When a blank sits beside a verb or an adjective, the answer is usually whatever that word *partners* with — not any word of similar meaning.

| Verb + noun | Adjective + noun | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| pay attention / compliments | staunch supporter | loyal follower |
| strike a balance / a bargain | soaring prices | rising fast |
| break the news / a record | grave mistake / crisis | very serious |
| take place / pride / measures | scathing attack | bitterly critical |
| make efforts / amends | teeming millions | crowds of people |
| do business / justice / harm | invaluable service | too valuable to price |
| commit a mistake / a crime | abject poverty | utter, hopeless |
| reach a conclusion / a consensus | conclusive evidence | settling the issue |
| cast a vote / a glance | close scrutiny | careful examination |
| lay emphasis / claim / hands on | level playing field | fair conditions |
| gain ground / momentum | glaring error | shockingly obvious |
| bear fruit / a resemblance | barren land / effort | unproductive |

**How to use the governor.** Identify the word immediately governing the blank:
- blank after a verb → the verb's usual object (*break the news*, *take place*);
- blank before a noun → the noun's usual adjective (*grave mistake*, *close scrutiny*);
- blank after a noun → its usual verb (*prices soar*, *attention pays*? — attention takes *pay*).

**Why collocation beats meaning.** 'made a mistake' and 'committed a mistake' both 'make sense', but SSC's standard answer follows the strongest partnership (*commit a mistake*, *commit a crime*). Similarly *reach* a conclusion (not *arrive* a conclusion), *pay* attention (not *give* attention), *heavy* rain (not *strong* rain).

**Register check.** When two partnerships both exist, the neutral-formal one fits SSC prose: *hold talks* beats *hold chats*; *offer condolences* beats *give sorrows* (which is not even an English partnership).

Build your pairing instinct in two weeks: one table of 10 pairs a day, and each pair immediately used in a sentence of your own. Recognition in the exam comes from *having produced* the pair once, not from having read it.

tricks.title: Governor-first reading
tricks.body: Read the sentence up to the blank, stop, and ask: 'What does this word usually take next?' Answer from memory, then look at the options — your answer is usually sitting there verbatim.

example.q: The two leaders held detailed ___ on the border dispute.
example.solution: 'held detailed...' asks for a discussion noun → *deliberations*. Celebrations/medications are topic-inappropriate; 'reverberations' is sound.

tricks.title: Topic veto
tricks.body: Collocation options in SSC are often same-suffix decoys (-tions, -ments). Kill them by topic first: a border dispute invites *talks/deliberations*, never *medications*.

tricks.title: Verb-object completeness
tricks.body: For verb blanks, complete the object in your head: 'attention is ___' → paid. If your completing verb is an option, mark it and move on.

mistakes: Choosing a synonym that breaks the partnership ('pay attention' → 'give attention').
Being impressed by long words; the collocation answer is usually the ordinary word.
Ignoring the preposition that follows the blank ('deliberations on', 'effect on').
Confusing adjective–noun order: the blank's side tells you its part of speech.
subtopics.notes:
### What a collocation blank really tests
The sentence is grammatically complete with almost every option — *give attention, do attention, make attention* all parse. What decides the answer is partnership: English fixes which word teams up with which. You are not choosing the best word; you are recognising the only word that native usage allows.

### The verb + noun swaps that papers love
- **pay** attention / a visit / a compliment / heed — never give, do or make.
- **take** place / a decision / a step / a risk — never give or do.
- **make** a mistake / progress / an effort / a noise — never do.
- **do** harm / good / a favour / one's duty — never make.
- **commit** a mistake / a crime / an error (formal register) — the decoy is *did*.
- **catch** a cold / a thief / a signal; **keep** a promise / a secret; **break** a promise / the news; **burst** into tears / into laughter; **reach** a conclusion / a verdict; **meet** a deadline / a requirement; **strike** a balance / a deal.

Drill them as whole chunks — never as verb + blank.

### Adjective + noun pairs
**heavy** rain / traffic; **strong** wind / coffee / odour; **fast** asleep; **sound** sleep; **narrow** escape / margin / victory; **close** shave / contest; **grave** mistake / risk; **solemn** pledge / promise; **stark** contrast / reality; **loud** applause. The planted decoys are near-synonyms that refuse the slot: *strong rain, quick asleep, tight escape* — wrong even though they look plausible.

### Prepositional collocations
When the blank sits before or after a fixed preposition, the chunk is the answer: emphasis **on**, comply **with**, abide **by**, capable **of**, fond **of**, congratulate somebody **on**, insist **on**, married **to**, superior **to**, deal **in** (trade) vs deal **with** (handle). The sentence gives you the preposition; only one word completes the pair.

### Register and fixedness
Some partnerships are frozen: *null and void, part and parcel, safe and sound, first and foremost* — no word can be swapped in. Others allow near-synonyms in free writing (*reach/arrive at a decision*) but the exam plays it safe: if an option set contains two real collocates, the setter has usually locked the context with a phrase or a preposition elsewhere in the sentence — read the WHOLE sentence before answering.

### How to train
Ten chunks a day, tested in both directions (verb → partner, partner → verb). In the exam, say the completed sentence silently: *give attention to the instructions* — no trained ear accepts it. The chunk either rings whole or it does not; hesitation means the partnership was never learnt.

### Quick revision
- pay attention/heed; take place/step; make a mistake/progress; do harm/good; commit a crime.
- heavy rain, strong wind, fast asleep, narrow escape, solemn pledge, stark contrast.
- The preposition in the sentence fixes the chunk: emphasis ON, comply WITH, capable OF.
- Frozen pairs (null and void, part and parcel) accept no substitutes.
- Say the sentence silently — the chunk rings whole or it does not.

patterns.name: do / make / take / give / pay verb swap
patterns.howToSpot: The blank is a verb before a noun like attention, place, a visit, a decision; the options are the swap-family (pay, give, do, make, take).
patterns.logic:
1. Read the noun after the blank — attention, place, visit are the tells.
2. Recall the chunk: pay attention, take place, pay a visit, take a decision.
3. Reject options that parse but do not partner: *give attention*, *do a visit*, *make place* are all un-English.

*Why it works:* the do/make/take family all fit grammar; only the fixed chunk fits usage, and the exam is testing exactly that.

example.q: Please ___ attention to the instructions before the demo begins.
example.solution: **pay** attention — the chunk is pay attention; give, do and make attention are all un-English.

patterns.name: Adjective + noun partnership
patterns.howToSpot: The blank is an adjective before rain, escape, sleep, pledge; the options are near-synonym adjectives (heavy/strong, narrow/close, fast/quick).
patterns.logic:
1. Name the noun that follows the blank.
2. Fetch the fixed partner: heavy rain, narrow escape, fast asleep, solemn pledge.
3. Test the decoys aloud — strong rain, quick asleep are the classic near-misses.

*Why it works:* near-synonyms are chosen because they sound almost right; the fixed partnership is the only defence.

example.q: The trekkers were caught in ___ rain on the third day.
example.solution: **heavy** rain — rain partners heavy; strong rain and powerful rain are not idiomatic.

patterns.name: Event and body-reaction collocations
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence describes illness, emotion or sudden reaction (a cold, tears, laughter); options are movement verbs (catch/burst vs take/rush).
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the event: falling ill, crying, laughing.
2. Fetch the chunk: catch a cold, burst into tears, burst into laughter.
3. Reject literal substitutes — take a cold, rush into tears are not idioms.

*Why it works:* these reaction chunks are frozen metaphors; the exam banks on candidates literalising them.

example.q: She ___ into tears when the results were announced.
example.solution: **burst** into tears — the fixed reaction chunk; break, rush and dash into tears are un-idiomatic.

patterns.name: Frozen idiomatic expressions
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence hints at news, escape or an event that must be phrased idiomatically (break the news, a narrow escape); one option completes the idiom.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the whole sentence for the situation: delivering bad news, escaping by inches.
2. Match the frozen expression: break the news (to), a narrow escape.
3. Reject synonym swaps — crack the news, thin escape are not the idiom.

*Why it works:* idioms are single vocabulary items written as several words; partial recall produces the planted decoys.

example.q: The manager had to ___ the news of the layoffs to the staff.
example.solution: **break** the news — the idiom for delivering unwelcome information; crack, tear and split the news do not exist.

patterns.name: reach / meet / strike outcome verbs
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits before an outcome noun (a balance, a deadline, a conclusion, a verdict); the options are hitting-class verbs (strike, hit, knock, beat).
patterns.logic:
1. Name the outcome noun.
2. Fetch the chunk: strike a balance, meet a deadline, reach a conclusion, arrive at a decision.
3. Check the prepositions around the blank — meet THE deadline (no preposition), arrive AT a decision.

*Why it works:* outcome verbs look interchangeable but each has a locked partner; the decoys are physical verbs applied literally.

example.q: The team worked over the weekend to ___ the submission deadline.
example.solution: **meet** the deadline — the fixed partnership; match, catch and equal a deadline are not idiomatic.

subtopics.title: Phrasal-verb blanks: verb + particle as one unit
subtopics.concept:
A phrasal verb is verb + particle(s) whose meaning is not the sum of its parts. Blanks here test whether you own the unit.

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Sentence cue |
|---|---|---|
| call off | cancel | the strike was called off |
| put up with | tolerate | she cannot put up with noise |
| carry out | perform, execute | carry out orders / a survey |
| break out | begin suddenly | a fire broke out |
| look into | investigate | the panel will look into it |
| turn down | reject | he turned down the offer |
| give in | surrender | the rebels finally gave in |
| run out of | exhaust the stock of | we ran out of time |
| do away with | abolish | the tax was done away with |
| bring about | cause to happen | the reform brought about change |
| cut down on | reduce | cut down on sugar |
| stand by | support; remain loyal | she stood by her friend |

**Two shapes of the blank.** Sometimes the particle is blanked ('call ___ the merger') and the verb is given; sometimes the whole unit is blanked among look-alike verbs ('___ up with the noise'). In both, the sentence's *action* decides:
- cancelling → call **off**;
- enduring → put **up with**;
- rejecting → turn **down**;
- abolishing → do away **with**.

**Particles carry direction.** *off* = cancel/away, *out* = erupt/distribute, *up* = appear/build, *down* = reject/reduce, *in* = surrender/enter. When two particles both look grammatical, this direction sense separates them.

**Transitive or not.** *Put up with* needs an object ('put up with the noise'); *give in* needs none ('the rebels gave in'). If the blank follows a ready object, a transitive unit is the answer; if the sentence ends at the blank, an intransitive one.

**Separable units.** 'called the meeting off' and 'called off the meeting' are both valid — so if the object sits between the blank's verb and particle, the unit is separable, and only that shape fits. Improvement items exploit this; fill-in items usually keep the unit intact.

tricks.title: Name the action, then match the unit
tricks.body: Say the sentence's action in one plain word (cancelled, tolerated, abolished), then pick the phrasal unit that translates it. The wrong particles translate other actions.

example.q: The company had to call ___ the proposed merger after the audit.
example.solution: Action = cancel → call **off**. *Call up* telephones, *call for* demands, *call out* shouts — different verbs entirely.

tricks.title: Particle direction check
tricks.body: Ask what the sentence does to its object — kills it (off/out), raises it (up), lowers it (down), accepts it (in). Match the particle's direction to the verb's fate.

tricks.title: Simple-verb substitution
tricks.body: Replace each option with a one-word verb (call off = cancel). The option whose substitution keeps the sentence's meaning is the answer.

mistakes: Choosing the particle that follows the preposition logic of the first language.
Mixing *put up with* (tolerate) with *put off* (postpone) because both contain 'put'.
Reading only the clause containing the blank; the actor and time usually sit in the previous clause.
Forgetting that 'break out' (war, fire, disease) has no passive — 'was broken out' is impossible.
subtopics.notes:
### One verb, many meanings — the particle is the word
A phrasal verb is verb + particle acting as a single new word. *Call off* (cancel) has nothing to do with calling; *give in* (surrender) has nothing to do with giving. The blank is therefore a meaning blank: read the sentence, get the intended sense, then find the verb+particle that carries it.

### Same verb, different particles — the favourite frame
- **call off** cancel; **call on** urge/appeal to; **call for** demand/require; **call up** telephone; **call in** summon/withdraw.
- **look after** care for; **look into** investigate; **look forward to** anticipate with pleasure; **look down upon** despise; **look up to** admire; **look for** search.
- **put off** postpone; **put up with** tolerate; **put down** suppress/repress; **put across** communicate; **put out** extinguish.
- **turn down** reject; **turn up** appear; **turn out** prove to be; **turn over** hand over.
- **give in** (to) surrender; **give up** quit; **give away** reveal/donate; **give off** emit.

When the stem repeats one verb across options (call ___ / look ___), the real question is: which sense does THIS sentence need?

### The to-trap
Three particles are followed by to + gerund, not to + verb: **look forward to meeting**, **be used to working**, **object to paying**. The to here is a preposition. Papers plant an infinitive decoy; the blank itself may BE the particle: *I am looking ___ to hearing from you* → **forward**.

### Separable, inseparable, pronominal
- If the object is a pronoun and the phrasal verb is separable, the pronoun moves inside: *call the match off → call it off* (never *call off it*).
- Three-part verbs (put up with, look down upon, get away with, run out of) never separate: *put up with it*, not *put with it up*.
- When the blank is the particle itself, the verb already in the sentence fixes the answer — read backwards from the sense.

### Register
Neutral options beat fancy ones: exam keys prefer come across (find by chance) over encounter when the blank is a phrasal slot. If two options are both real phrasal verbs, only one carries the sentence's meaning — test each in place and let meaning, not familiarity, decide.

### Quick revision
- call off cancel; call on urge; call for demand; put off postpone; put up with tolerate; look into investigate; look after care for; turn down reject; give in to surrender.
- The sentence's sense picks the particle; the verb is already given.
- look forward TO + V-ing — to is a preposition there.
- Pronouns separate two-part verbs (call it off); three-part verbs never separate.
- Test every option in place; familiarity is not the test, meaning is.

patterns.name: Same verb, four particles
patterns.howToSpot: All options share the verb's particle slot around one repeated verb (called ___ / call ___): off, on, for, in, up.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the sentence and name the intended sense: cancel? urge? demand?
2. Match the sense to the particle: cancel → off; urge a person → on; demand → for; summon → in.
3. Re-read the completed sentence — the particle must make one natural whole.

*Why it works:* the four particles turn one verb into four unrelated words; the sentence's meaning is the only selector.

example.q: The board meeting has been ___ owing to the chairman's indisposition.
example.solution: **called off** — the sense is cancelled; called for would mean 'demanded', called up 'telephoned'.

patterns.name: look-family blanks
patterns.howToSpot: The verb look sits before the blank (or the blank is its particle); options are after, into, forward, down, up.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide the sense: caring → after; investigating → into; anticipating → forward to; despising → down upon.
2. If forward is chosen, confirm the sentence carries to + V-ing or a noun after to.
3. Reject particles that make real words with wrong senses.

*Why it works:* look is the most examined phrasal verb because its particles fan out into five everyday senses.

example.q: A three-member committee will look ___ the ragging complaint.
example.solution: **look into** — investigate; look after would mean the committee will care for the complaint.

patterns.name: put-family and toleration frames
patterns.howToSpot: Sentences about postponing, tolerating or enduring; the blank completes put ___ (with), or the options are off / up with / down / across.
patterns.logic:
1. Sense: postpone → off; tolerate → up with; communicate → across; suppress → down.
2. put up with is three parts — check the object sits after with.
3. Confirm the completed sentence reads as one natural verb.

*Why it works:* put is the second most-set phrasal verb, and its toleration sense (put up with) is the classic three-part trap.

example.q: The workers refused to put ___ the unsafe conditions any longer.
example.solution: **put up with** — tolerate; the three-part verb keeps its object after with.

patterns.name: Mixed high-frequency phrasal verbs
patterns.howToSpot: Options are four unrelated phrasal verbs (turned down / turned up / carried out / gave in), each with a different verb; the sentence must accept exactly one.
patterns.logic:
1. Paraphrase the sentence's needed sense in plain words: reject? surrender? perform?
2. Map to the phrasal verb: reject → turn down; surrender (to) → give in to; perform → carry out.
3. Check the tail: if the sentence continues with 'to', give in fits and give up does not.

*Why it works:* with unrelated verbs the options cannot be confused by shape — meaning and the surrounding words (a trailing to, an object) decide.

example.q: The college turned ___ his application because of the incomplete marks card.
example.solution: **turned down** — rejected; turned up would mean the application appeared by itself.

subtopics.title: Verb-form and tense blanks
subtopics.concept:
When the blank is a verb, two checks decide: the **anchor** (time information in the sentence) and the **form demanded by the governing word**.

**Anchors → tenses:**
- *By the time X arrived, ...* → the earlier event is past perfect: *had burnt*.
- *since 2015 / for ten years* (continuing) → present perfect (continuous).
- *yesterday / last week* → simple past.
- *by next March* → future perfect: *will have completed*.

**Governing words → forms (the highest-yield list):**
- *look forward to + -ing* (to = preposition): *I look forward to **hearing** from you*.
- *used to + base* (past habit) vs *be used to + -ing* (accustomed): *He used to **swim***; *He is used to **swimming***.
- *had better / would rather + base*: *You had better **leave***.
- *avoid / enjoy / mind / finish / suggest + -ing*.
- *decide / plan / hope / refuse + to + base*.
- preposition + -ing: *insisted on **paying***, *afraid of **losing***.

**The preposition-to test** settles most -ing vs to-blank confusion: if the word before 'to' is a noun, pronoun or preposition-like verb (look forward, be accustomed, object), the 'to' is prepositional → *-ing* follows. If 'to' belongs to an infinitive (decide, refuse, hope), the base verb follows.

**Passive shapes** also appear: after *by the time*, a completed earlier event can be *had been + participle* when the subject receives the action (*had been evacuated*).

tricks.title: Preposition-to test
tricks.body: Check what owns the 'to'. Owned by a preposition-verb or noun → -ing; owned by an infinitive verb → base form. This one test answers the largest tense-form family.

example.q: I look forward to ___ from you soon. → hearing
example.solution: 'Forward to' is prepositional ('look forward to it'), so the -ing form follows: *hearing*.

tricks.title: By-the-time ladder
tricks.body: Two events with 'by the time' → earlier verb in past perfect, later in simple past. Fit the blank to its rung of the ladder.

tricks.title: Verb-category lists
tricks.body: Memorise the three mini-lists: -ing verbs (avoid, enjoy, mind, suggest, finish), to-verbs (decide, hope, refuse, plan), base-after (had better, would rather, let, make).

mistakes: Choosing 'to hear' after 'look forward to' because 'to' feels infinitive.
Using present perfect with a finished-time anchor.
Writing 'used to + -ing' for past habits (that shape means 'accustomed').
Ignoring the passive when the sentence's subject receives the action.
subtopics.notes:
### Read the anchors first
A verb-form blank is solved by the time anchors around it: **since 2019, for a decade, by the time, already, yet, yesterday, before, after, when, if, until**. Circle the anchors, then let them pick the form. The wrong options are always well-formed verbs from the wrong row.

### The anchor map
- **since + point / for + length** → perfect territory: *has worked*, *has been working* (ongoing emphasis).
- **Two past events, one earlier** → the earlier one takes **had + V3**: *The train had left before we reached.* The before/after/when clause carries the LATER event in simple past.
- **by + future time** → will have + V3; **by + past time** → had + V3.
- **Hardly/Scarcely had ... when ... / No sooner had ... than ...** → the frame is past perfect + simple past, and the correlative pairs are fixed: no sooner→than, hardly/scarcely→when.
- **If (type 1)** → simple present in the if-clause, will + V1 in the main clause. **Had I known ...** (inverted type 3) → would have + V3. Will never enters the if-clause.

### Non-finite blanks
When the neighbouring word is a fixed verb or preposition, the form is fixed too:
- enjoy, avoid, deny, suggest, mind, finish + **V-ing**.
- want, decide, agree, refuse, hope + **to + V1**.
- Every preposition + **V-ing** (interested in learning).
- Negative infinitive = **not to + V1**; negative gerund = **not + V-ing**.
*He denied taking the file* — deny takes the gerund; 'denied to take' is the planted decoy.

### Agreement traps dressed as blanks
**Each of / every one of / either of / neither of + plural noun → singular verb**: *Each of the candidates has...*. **A number of + plural → plural**; **the number of + plural → singular**. Collective nouns take singular when the unit acts (*The jury has reached its verdict*). The blank may simply be is/has/does — agreement, not tense, decides.

### The elimination sweep
1. Kill forms that break the anchor (a present form beside yesterday).
2. Kill forms that break a fixed frame (will inside an if-clause; to after deny).
3. Kill agreement breaks (have after each of).
4. Among survivors, prefer the row that matches the sentence's aspect — ongoing (has been working) vs completed (has worked).

### Quick revision
- since/for → perfect; earlier past event → had + V3; later past event in the clause → simple past.
- no sooner ... than; hardly/scarcely ... when — past perfect + simple past.
- Type 1: present in the if-clause; Had I known → would have + V3.
- deny/enjoy/avoid + V-ing; want/decide/refuse + to + V1; preposition + V-ing.
- each of / neither of → singular verb; a number of → plural, the number of → singular.

patterns.name: since / for with perfect forms
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence carries since 2019, for a decade, all morning; the options mix simple present, present perfect and past perfect.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the anchor: since/for ties the action to the present.
2. Ongoing action → has/have been + V-ing; completed count → has/have + V3.
3. A pure past frame (before moving to..., yesterday) moves the row back to had + V3.

*Why it works:* since/for are the signature of the perfect rows; the options differ only by row, so the anchor settles it.

example.q: He ___ in this office since 2019.
example.solution: **has been working** — since 2019 keeps the action alive in the present, so the present perfect continuous row fits; 'worked' would detach it.

patterns.name: Past-perfect frame + simple past clause
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence has Hardly had ... when ..., or two past events with before/when; the blank is the second verb.
patterns.logic:
1. The had + V3 event is the earlier one; the blank event is the later one.
2. The later event takes the SIMPLE PAST in the when/before clause: went, started.
3. Reject had + V3 for the later event and present forms for both.

*Why it works:* the past perfect exists to mark the earlier of two past events; using it twice erases the very contrast it exists to draw.

example.q: The guests had hardly settled when the lights ___ out.
example.solution: **went** — the hardly-frame is past perfect + simple past: had settled ... went. 'Had gone' would claim both events at the same earlier level.

patterns.name: Conditional frames
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence opens with If or the inverted Had I...; options offer will inside the if-clause, or mix would/would have.
patterns.logic:
1. Type 1 (real): If + simple present, main clause will + V1 — will never enters the if-clause.
2. Type 3 (unreal past): Had + subject + V3 ... would have + V3.
3. Match the two halves — mixing a type-3 if with a type-1 result is the planted fault.

*Why it works:* each conditional type is a fixed two-row pattern; the options are rows from the wrong type.

example.q: Had I known about the schedule change, I ___ accordingly.
example.solution: **would have planned** — the inverted Had I known opens the unreal past; the result is would have + V3, never 'will plan' or plain 'would plan'.

patterns.name: Gerund vs infinitive after fixed verbs
patterns.howToSpot: The blank follows deny/enjoy/avoid/suggest (gerund) or want/decide/refuse/warn (infinitive); the options are to + V1, V-ing, and broken hybrids.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the word BEFORE the blank.
2. Gerund group: enjoy, avoid, deny, suggest, mind, finish, every preposition → V-ing.
3. Infinitive group: want, decide, agree, refuse, hope, warn (warn + object + not to V1) → to + V1.

*Why it works:* the first verb's fixed group decides the form; no meaning test is needed once the group is known.

example.q: He denied ___ the confidential file.
example.solution: **taking** — deny takes the gerund; 'denied to take' is the planted decoy.

patterns.name: Agreement blanks (each of, the number of)
patterns.howToSpot: The subject phrase is each of / either of / the number of + a plural noun, and the options are has/have, is/are type pairs.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the true head of the subject: each, either, the number — all singular.
2. Choose the singular verb (has, is, was) whatever plural noun follows.
3. Contrast: a number of + plural noun → plural verb.

*Why it works:* the plural noun is camouflage; agreement follows the head word, and the options exist to punish head-hunting laziness.

example.q: Each of the shortlisted candidates ___ to bring the originals.
example.solution: **has** — each is the head, singular; 'have' agrees with the nearest noun, the classic trap.

subtopics.title: Connective and relative-pronoun blanks
subtopics.concept:
Connective blanks join two clauses; the relation between the clauses, not the meaning of any single word, is the answer.

| Pair | Fixed shape | Trap option |
|---|---|---|
| Hardly / Scarcely ... when | Hardly had she entered **when** the lights went out. | **than** (belongs to no sooner) |
| No sooner ... than | No sooner had he sat down **than**... | **when** |
| Not only ... but also | not only cheap **but also** durable | but, and |
| Both ... and | **Both** the manager **and** his staff were present | as well as |
| Rather ... than | would resign **rather than** apologize | then |
| Too ... to | **too** weak **to** walk | so, very |
| So ... that | **so** weak **that** he could not walk | too |
| Lest ... should | run fast **lest** you **should** miss it | or else |

**The +/- test again:** give each clause a direction. Same directions → *so/therefore/and*; opposite → *but/yet/although*; explanation → *because/since*; outcome → *so/therefore*. For fixed pairs, both halves must appear: 'Hardly had... **when**', 'No sooner had... **than**' — the trap options simply swap the partners.

**Relative pronouns.** The blank joining a describing clause to its noun:
- person + subject role → **who** (*the leader **who** inspires*);
- person + object role → **whom** (*the leader **whom** everyone trusts* — test by rephrasing: *everyone trusts him*);
- possession → **whose**; things → **which/that**;
- place → **where**; time → **when**; reason → **why**.
The he/him substitution is foolproof: replace the pronoun's slot with he (→ who) or him (→ whom).

**Concessive pairs:** *Although/Though* pairs with *yet* (never *but*): 'Although it rained, **yet** the match continued' is standard formal usage; SSC accepts plain 'Although... the match continued' equally. *Despite/In spite of* take noun/-ing, never a full clause ('despite it rained' is wrong).

tricks.title: Partner scan before choosing
tricks.body: Search the sentence for the other half of the pair. Seeing 'Hardly had' fixes the blank to *when*; seeing 'No sooner' fixes it to *than*. Zero deliberation needed.

example.q: Hardly had she entered the room ___ the lights went out.
example.solution: 'Hardly had...' → partner **when**. *Than* belongs to 'No sooner'.

tricks.title: He/him substitution for who/whom
tricks.body: Rephrase the clause with he/him: 'everyone trusts (him)' → whom; '(he) inspires everyone' → who. No ambiguity survives the substitution.

tricks.title: Despite/Although sorting
tricks.body: Full clause after the blank → Although/Though; noun or -ing → Despite/In spite of. The trap options swap these two families.

mistakes: Choosing 'than' after 'Hardly/Scarcely' because 'comparison' instinct fires.
Using 'whom' as a clause subject ('the man whom came') — case is decided by the clause role, not by prestige.
Joining a full clause with 'despite' or a bare noun with 'although'.
Selecting 'which' for a person or 'who' for a thing under time pressure.
subtopics.notes:
### Connectives are logic blanks
The sentence is complete on both sides of the blank; the option only decides the RELATIONSHIP between the two sides — contrast, cause, time, addition, condition. Read both clauses, label their relationship in plain words (He rehearsed BUT forgot; The flights were delayed BECAUSE of fog), then pick the option that spells that label.

### The correlative pairs (fixed partners)
- **No sooner ... than** (and it inverts: No sooner had he sat down than...).
- **Hardly / Scarcely ... when**.
- **Both ... and; Either ... or; Neither ... nor; Not only ... but also** — these come as pair-options in double blanks; the partners must travel together.
- **so ... that; such ... that; as ... as; between ... and; from ... to**.
Mixing the partners (no sooner ... when) is a planted fault.

### Relative pronouns: case, not taste
- **who** does the action (people); **whom** receives it; **whose** shows possession (also for buildings: a house whose roof...).
- **which** for things and for non-identifying clauses after a comma — *that* never follows a comma.
- **that** for identifying clauses of people or things.
- **what** = the thing that (no antecedent before it).
Quick case test: rewrite the clause as a sentence — *The engineer won the award* → The engineer **who** won the award.

### Reflexives and each other
- Reflexive: myself, themselves — the doer and receiver are the same (The children arranged the hall **themselves**).
- each other / one another: reciprocal action between different parties.
- Papers plant *theirselves / themself* — non-words — and *hisself*.

### Contrast and cause: the commonest options
**Although / Though / Even though** + clause; **Despite / In spite of** + noun phrase (never a bare clause). **Because + clause; because of / owing to / due to + noun**. **However** needs its own sentence rhythm (semicolon or new sentence); **therefore / hence / consequently** draw conclusions; **moreover / besides** add; **otherwise** gives the negative consequence. Most wrong options are right words with the wrong grammar after them — although the rain (wrong) vs despite the rain (right).

### Quick revision
- Label the relationship first: contrast, cause, time, addition, condition.
- Fixed pairs: no sooner...than; hardly...when; both...and; neither...nor; not only...but also.
- who acts, whom receives, whose possesses; which after a comma, never that.
- despite / in spite of + noun; although / though + clause.
- themselves (not theirselves); each other for mutual action.

patterns.name: Correlative time frames (no sooner ... than)
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence already opens with No sooner had / Hardly had / Scarcely had and the blank is the second partner; options are than, when, then, that.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the first partner: no sooner → than; hardly/scarcely → when.
2. Reject then (a time adverb, not a correlative) and that (a statement connector).
3. Confirm the frame's tense pairing — past perfect first clause, simple past second.

*Why it works:* the partners are frozen; every other option is a look-alike connector from a different frame.

example.q: No sooner had the bell rung ___ the students rushed out.
example.solution: **than** — the partner of no sooner is always than; 'when' belongs to hardly/scarcely.

patterns.name: Relative pronoun by case
patterns.howToSpot: The blank joins a noun to a clause; options are who / whom / whose / which / that.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the antecedent (person or thing) and the pronoun's job inside the clause.
2. Subject of the clause → who (people) / which (things); object → whom; possession → whose.
3. After a comma, only which/who survive — that is banned in non-identifying clauses.

*Why it works:* rewriting the clause as a standalone sentence exposes the pronoun's case in seconds.

example.q: The engineer ___ designed the bridge won a national award.
example.solution: **who** — the pronoun is the subject of 'designed'; whom would need an object role, whose needs possession.

patterns.name: Contrast and cause connectives
patterns.howToSpot: Two complete clauses stand on either side of the blank; the options are although / because / therefore / however type connectors.
patterns.logic:
1. Label the relationship: the second clause contradicts → contrast; explains → cause; concludes → result.
2. Contrast + clause → although/though; cause → because; conclusion → therefore/thus.
3. Check the grammar after the option: despite/in spite of demand a noun phrase, not a clause.

*Why it works:* the logic label is unambiguous once both clauses are read; the options are one connector per relationship.

example.q: ___ he had rehearsed for weeks, he forgot his lines on stage.
example.solution: **Although** — the second clause contradicts the first; Because would give cause and ruin the sense.

patterns.name: Possessive and reflexive pronouns
patterns.howToSpot: Options are whose / who's, themselves / theirselves, its / it's — form-pairs differing by an apostrophe or a suffix.
patterns.logic:
1. Possession before a noun → whose (the possessive has no apostrophe); who's = who is.
2. Same doer and receiver → reflexive: themselves, myself (never theirselves/hisself).
3. its = possession; it's = it is — expand and test.

*Why it works:* the apostrophe pairs are sound-alikes; expanding them (who is, it is) settles the case mechanically.

example.q: The athlete, ___ dedication is legendary, trains at dawn.
example.solution: **whose** — the clause possesses the dedication; who's would mean 'who is dedication', which is meaningless.

patterns.name: despite / although grammar match
patterns.howToSpot: The blank introduces a contrasting element; the giveaway is what FOLLOWS the blank — a noun phrase or a full clause with a verb.
patterns.logic:
1. Noun phrase / V-ing after the blank → despite or in spite of.
2. Full clause (subject + verb) → although / though / even though.
3. Never mix: 'despite it rained' and 'although the rain' are the two planted hybrids.

*Why it works:* the two contrast families differ only in the grammar they demand, which makes the following words decisive.

example.q: ___ the heavy downpour, the match went on.
example.solution: **Despite** — a noun phrase follows; Although would need a clause ('although it rained heavily').

subtopics.title: Confusable and homonym blanks
subtopics.concept:
These blanks offer four words of similar shape; only one fits both the grammar slot and the meaning.

| Pair | Meanings | Correct use |
|---|---|---|
| affect / effect | verb: influence / noun: result | Rains **affect** crops; the **effect** was visible. |
| advice / advise | noun (an advice) / verb (to advise) | The doctor **advised** rest; follow his **advice**. |
| practice / practise | noun (Indian English) / verb | Daily **practice** helps; **practise** daily. |
| principal / principle | chief, head / a rule | **Principal** amount; a man of **principle**. |
| stationary / stationery | not moving / writing materials | a **stationary** van; office **stationery**. |
| loose / lose | not tight / misplace | a **loose** tooth; **lose** the keys. |
| site / sight / cite | place / vision / quote | a construction **site**; at first **sight**; **cite** a case. |
| complement / compliment | completes / praise | wine **complements** food; pay a **compliment**. |
| discreet / discrete | careful / separate | **discreet** enquiries; **discrete** units. |
| eligible / illegible | qualified / unreadable | **eligible** voters; **illegible** signature. |
| beside / besides | next to / in addition to | sat **beside** me; **besides** swimming. |
| assure / ensure / insure | remove doubt / make certain / cover by policy | **assure** the public; **ensure** safety; **insure** the car. |
| lie / lay | recline (lie–lay–lain) / put (lay–laid) | **lie** down; **lay** the pen on the table. |

**Two-step decision.**
1. **Part of speech.** *advise* (verb) vs *advice* (noun): find the sentence's verb — if it already has one, the blank is likely a noun, and vice versa. Same for *practice/practise*, *effect/affect* (noun vs verb).
2. **Meaning.** *stationary* (not moving) vs *stationery* (writing material); *principal* (chief) vs *principle* (rule). The sentence's context — a godown of paper goods, a bank's sums — picks one.

**Spelling-distinct pairs with one meaning slot:** *eligible* (qualified) vs *illegible* (unreadable); *discreet* (careful) vs *discrete* (separate); *complement* (completes) vs *compliment* (praise). Meaning decides alone.

**The assure/ensure/insure family** deserves its own memorisation: *assure* a person (remove doubt), *ensure* an outcome (make certain), *insure* a thing (insurance policy). 'The minister gave a solemn **assurance**' is the noun of *assure* — options include *insurance* to trap the shape-reader.

**Sound-alike traps in options** (affection, effectiveness, advices) exist to punish incomplete reading: reject them on grammar ('advices' is not a countable noun in standard English) and on meaning.

tricks.title: Slot first, meaning second
tricks.body: Decide noun/verb/adjective from the sentence frame; kill every option of the wrong class. Then choose by meaning among survivors — usually only two ever reach step two.

example.q: The doctor ___ him to take complete rest. Options: advised / advice / advices / advise.
example.solution: The sentence needs a finite past verb (subject 'doctor', no other verb) → **advised**. *Advice* is a noun, *advices* is not standard, *advise* is the wrong tense/number fit here.

tricks.title: Context picture
tricks.body: Form a mental image of the sentence: a pile of paper in a godown → stationery; a parked van → stationary. The image picks the spelling instantly.

tricks.title: Triple-family cards
tricks.body: Make flash cards only for families of three or more: assure/ensure/insure, site/sight/cite, affect/effect/affective. Singles rarely appear in options.

mistakes: Choosing the familiar spelling ('affect') when the slot demands the noun ('effect').
Reading 'advice/advise' as interchangeable because dictionaries mark the Indian-English overlap.
Picking 'illegible' for eligibility contexts because the negative prefix sounds right.
Missing that the sentence already has a verb, so the blank must be a noun.
subtopics.notes:
### Sound-alike, sense-apart
Confusable blanks offer pairs that differ by one letter or one sound: advice/advise, lose/loose, stationary/stationery, principal/principle, censor/censure, allusion/illusion. Grammar cannot help — *The minister gave a solemn advise* parses as words — but meaning can. Decide what the sentence must SAY, then take the word whose part of speech and meaning match.

### The noun/verb twins
- **advice** (noun) / **advise** (verb): sound *advice*; doctors *advise*.
- **practice** (noun) / **practise** (verb, British spelling): medical *practice*; lawyers *practise*.
- **licence** (noun) / **license** (verb): a driving *licence*; premises *licensed*.
- **belief** (noun) / **believe** (verb); **proof** (noun) / **prove** (verb); **bath** (noun) / **bathe** (verb).
These -ce (noun) / -se (verb) pairs are recycled endlessly. If the blank follows a or the, the noun is wanted; if it follows to or a subject, the verb.

### The meaning twins
- **lose** (misplace, fail to win) / **loose** (not tight): *come loose*, *lose the keys*.
- **affect** (verb, influence) / **effect** (noun, result; also verb = bring about): *will affect schedules*, *had an effect*.
- **stationary** (still) / **stationery** (writing materials).
- **principal** (chief, head; also the money) / **principle** (rule, belief).
- **complement** (completes) / **compliment** (praise).
- **allusion** (reference) / **illusion** (false perception) / **elusion** (escape).
- **censure** (rebuke) / **censor** (ban content).
- **continual** (repeated with breaks) / **continuous** (unbroken).
- **practicable** (workable) / **practical** (useful in practice).
- **personnel** (staff) / **personal** (private).

### The two-second test
Ask: what part of speech is the blank? Noun slots (after the, a, his, solemn...) take the -ce/-ency/-ion noun; verb slots (after to, will, did) take the -se/-ise verb. If both options are nouns, switch to meaning: still vs paper? rule vs person? praise vs rebuke? The sentence always contains one clue word that forces the choice — find it before reading the options.

### Why these are free marks
Unlike collocations, confusables have no grey zone: only one member of each pair means what the sentence needs. One careful read beats guesswork; the decoys exist purely for candidates answering on shape-memory.

### Quick revision
- advice/practice/licence = nouns; advise/practise/license = verbs (British usage) — check the slot.
- lose = misplace; loose = not tight. affect = verb; effect = noun (usually).
- stationary still; stationery pens. principal = head, chief or capital sum; principle = rule or belief.
- censure = rebuke; censor = ban. allusion = reference; illusion = mirage.
- continual = repeated; continuous = unbroken. personnel = staff; personal = private.

patterns.name: Noun/verb twins (-ce vs -se)
patterns.howToSpot: Options are advice/advise, practice/practise, licence/license type pairs; the blank follows an article or a subject respectively.
patterns.logic:
1. Fix the part of speech the slot needs: after the/a/his → noun; after to / a subject → verb.
2. Take the matching twin: advice (n) vs advise (v); practise (v) vs practice (n).
3. Read back — the completed phrase must be a standard unit (sound advice, advise somebody).

*Why it works:* the twins share sound and differ only in class; the slot's neighbours (article vs to) already announce the class.

example.q: The dietician gave me sound ___ on portion control.
example.solution: **advice** — the noun is wanted after 'gave me sound'; 'advise' is a verb and cannot follow the adjective 'sound'.

patterns.name: lose / loose and affect / effect
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence is about misplacing, tightness, influence or results; the options are the two shape-twins plus derivatives.
patterns.logic:
1. lose = fail to keep; loose = not tight — test the sense, not the spelling.
2. affect = verb (influence); effect = noun (result). Will/can before the blank → affect; an/the before it → effect.
3. Derivative decoys (affection, effectively) die on meaning.

*Why it works:* the pairs are one-letter apart, so shape-memory fails by design; the sentence's verb or article gives the class away.

example.q: The new timings will ___ train schedules across the zone.
example.solution: **affect** — the verb (influence) is wanted after will; 'effect' as a verb would mean bring about, and the noun cannot follow will alone.

patterns.name: stationary / stationery and principal / principle
patterns.howToSpot: Sentences about offices, shops, movement, rules or people in charge; options are the twin spellings.
patterns.logic:
1. Paper-and-pen sense → stationery; motionless → stationary.
2. A rule or moral standard → principle; the head, the chief, the capital sum → principal.
3. The -ar / -er ending is the memory hook: stationERy = papER, principlE = rulE.

*Why it works:* the twins differ by one letter with totally different meanings; the clue word (shop, head, rule) forces the choice.

example.q: The office buys its ___ from the shop near the station.
example.solution: **stationery** — writing materials; 'stationary' would have the office buying stillness.

patterns.name: censure / censor and allusion / illusion
patterns.howToSpot: Sentences about parliament, books, films, references or appearances; options are the paired look-alikes.
patterns.logic:
1. Formal rebuke → censure; banning or cutting content → censor.
2. A reference to something → allusion; a false appearance → illusion; a slipping away → elusion.
3. Match the register marker in the sentence (House, minister, poem) to the word's home territory.

*Why it works:* both pairs live in formal writing, so the decoy always sounds educated; the sense — rebuke vs ban, reference vs mirage — is the only sieve.

example.q: The House ___ the minister for his careless remark.
example.solution: **censured** — the House rebukes; censoring belongs to content, not to conduct.

subtopics.title: Double blanks: two gaps, one sentence
subtopics.concept:
Some items blank two positions in one sentence — a pair of connectors (*___ he was ill, ___ he came*), a structure pair (*too ... to*, *so ... that*), or two content words. Options are complete pairs.

**Method: anchor the solid blank first.** One of the two gaps is usually much easier — a structure pair whose second element is fixed (*too ___ to*), or a content word only one option can fit. Decide that gap, and the wrong pairs collapse:
- '*___ small ___ accommodate*' → the structure is *too + adj + to + verb* → **too, to**. 'So, that' would need a clause ('so small that it could not accommodate'), and the option's second element ('that') does not fit the blank before the bare verb.
- '*___ the manager ___ his assistants were present*' → plural *were* + two-part subject → **Both, and**. 'Neither, or' is not a pair; 'Either, or' would demand singular agreement.

**Agreement as a tiebreak.** The sentence's verb exposes the pair: plural verb → *both... and* (or a plural pair), singular verb → *either... or / neither... nor* (verb follows the nearer noun).

**Cross-check both halves.** After anchoring one blank, read the completed sentence aloud; if the second half jars, your anchor was the trap — the option pairs are built so that exactly one completes both halves naturally.

**Content-word pairs** (e.g. '*safe and sound*', '*part and parcel*') are fixed binomials — learn the common ones in pairs, never singly: *safe and sound, first and foremost, null and void, ways and means, pros and cons, part and parcel*.

tricks.title: Structure-pair recognition
tricks.body: too + adjective + to + base verb; so + adjective + that + clause; such + noun + that + clause; hardly...when; no sooner...than. Recognise the skeleton and both blanks fill at once.

example.q: The room was ___ small ___ accommodate all the guests.
example.solution: Adjective + bare verb after the second blank → *too small to accommodate*. 'So, that' would demand 'that it could not accommodate'.

tricks.title: Verb-agreement tiebreak
tricks.body: Plural verb with two subjects → Both...and; singular verb → Either...or / Neither...nor (matching the nearer noun). The verb alone often fixes the pair.

tricks.title: Fixed binomial bank
tricks.body: Revise binomials in pairs: safe and sound, part and parcel, null and void, first and foremost, ways and means. Options split genuine binomials with a wrong partner — the genuine one is the answer.

mistakes: Solving blank two first when blank one is the structural anchor.
Choosing 'so, that' where the second blank precedes a bare verb (structure mismatch).
Matching plural 'Both...and' to a singular-verb sentence.
Assembling a binomial that half-exists ('part and half') because the first half matched.
subtopics.notes:
### Two gaps, one decision
A double blank is still one choice: the options are complete PAIRS (both ... and / neither ... nor / null and void), so you test the whole pair in place. Never solve gap one and glance at gap two — the pair that fits gap one may fail gap two, which is exactly where the planted decoy lives.

### Grammar-locked pairs
When the options are correlatives, the verb's number or the sentence's structure can settle it alone:
- **Both ... and** → plural verb (Both the pilot and the co-pilot **were** honoured).
- **Neither ... nor / Either ... or** → the verb agrees with the NEARER subject (Neither the boys nor the coach **was** told).
- **Not only ... but also** → the second half carries new, added information.
So read the unblanked verb first — *were honoured* announces Both ... and; *was punished* announces Either/Neither.

### Sense-locked pairs
Other double blanks lock by meaning, not grammar: *Neither his age nor his frail health could stop him — and he finished the marathon.* The tail clause confirms the sense, and only one pair survives. In these items, read to the full stop before choosing; the confirmation clause is the setter's gift.

### Fixed expressions printed as pairs
A whole family of idioms is two words long: **null and void** (invalid), **part and parcel** (an essential part), **safe and sound**, **first and foremost**, **odds and ends**, **done and dusted** (finished), **one and all** (everyone). Here the options are competing expressions and only one matches the sentence's meaning; the second blank is just the idiom's second half.

### Time-span and range pairs
**from ... to** marks a range (from Monday to Friday); **between ... and** links exactly two items; **scarcely ... when / no sooner ... than** report near-simultaneous events. Again the partner is fixed: from never pairs with and, no sooner never pairs with when. Sweep the pair, not the single word.

### The protocol
1. Read the full sentence including the tail after the second blank.
2. Test each pair IN PLACE, both halves.
3. Let grammar (the unblanked verb's number) kill pairs first, then sense.
4. Among survivors, prefer the more precise idiom or correlative — never the one that merely sounds grand.

### Quick revision
- Solve PAIRS, never single blanks: test both halves in place.
- both...and → plural verb; neither/either...or/nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject.
- The tail clause after the second blank usually locks the sense — read to the full stop.
- null and void, part and parcel, safe and sound, done and dusted — fixed, unswappable.
- from...to, between...and, no sooner...than, scarcely...when — fixed partners, no mixing.

patterns.name: Correlative pair blanks (both/neither/either)
patterns.howToSpot: Two blanks frame two nouns with one verb visible; the options are both...and / either...or / neither...nor / not only...but also.
patterns.logic:
1. Check the unblanked verb's number: were → both...and; was → neither/either; an added second fact → not only...but also.
2. Then check sense: exclusion → neither...nor; choice → either...or.
3. Read the tail clause for confirmation where grammar allows two pairs.

*Why it works:* the correlative dictates the verb's number, so the unblanked half of the sentence often answers before the options are read.

example.q: ___ the pilot ___ the co-pilot were honoured for the emergency landing.
example.solution: **Both ... and** — the plural 'were honoured' demands both...and; neither/either would need 'was'.

patterns.name: Fixed two-word idioms
patterns.howToSpot: The options are whole expressions (null and void, part and parcel, safe and sound); the sentence describes invalidity, essentiality or safety.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the sentence's message: cancelled/invalid, essential, unhurt, finished.
2. Match the idiom: null and void; part and parcel; safe and sound; done and dusted.
3. Reject idioms that are real but mean something else — they are the decoys.

*Why it works:* each option is a genuine idiom, so only meaning separates them; the sentence's key noun or verb is the sieve.

example.q: The old agreement was declared ___ after the merger.
example.solution: **null and void** — legally invalid; 'part and parcel' would call the agreement essential, the opposite.

patterns.name: Range and link pairs (from...to, between...and)
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence spans a time range or links exactly two parties; options are preposition pairs.
patterns.logic:
1. Range (start ... end) → from ... to.
2. Exactly two linked parties → between ... and; three or more → among.
3. Confirm the pair's grammar — from never partners with and, between never with to.

*Why it works:* the pairs are fixed by convention; the decoys mix partners that never travel together.

example.q: The summer sale runs ___ 1 May ___ 15 May.
example.solution: **from ... to** — the fixed range pair; 'from ... and' and 'between ... to' mix partners that never travel together.

patterns.name: Hardly / no sooner paired frames
patterns.howToSpot: The sentence opens with a fronted adverb frame and the blank completes it: options carry the second partner (than, when, then).
patterns.logic:
1. No sooner → than; hardly/scarcely → when. The pairs never cross.
2. then and that are never partners — they are pure decoys.
3. Expect the past perfect + simple past sequence around the frame.

*Why it works:* the frame is a memorised unit; the options only test whether the candidate memorised it whole.

example.q: ___ had the plane touched down ___ the passengers began applauding.
example.solution: **No sooner ... than** — the fixed partner; 'hardly ... than' and 'no sooner ... when' are the planted mixed pairs.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The blank is a verb before a noun such as attention, place, a mistake or a decision; the options are do / make / take / give / pay.
pyqPatterns.approach: Read the noun first and recall the fixed chunk: pay attention, take place, make a mistake, do harm, commit a crime. Say the whole chunk silently — only one option sounds natural with that noun.

example.q: The annual sports meet will ___ place in the second week of December.
example.solution: **take** place — the fixed chunk for an event happening; give, make and hold place are not idiomatic.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The blank is an adjective before rain, escape, traffic or asleep, or it completes a frozen idiom (part and parcel, hold water); the options are near-synonyms.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fetch the fixed partner (heavy rain, narrow escape, fast asleep). Near-synonyms such as strong, thin or quick are planted because they mean almost the same thing but never partner the noun.

example.q: The bus driver had a ___ escape when the truck swerved into his lane.
example.solution: **narrow** escape — thin, slim and tight mean small but are not the partner of escape.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options are look-alikes: advice/advise, affect/effect, stationary/stationery, principal/principle, allusion/illusion.
pyqPatterns.approach: First work out which part of speech the slot needs (after a/the -> noun; after a subject, can or will -> verb), then the meaning (still vs paper, head vs rule). One clue word in the sentence always decides it.

example.q: Lack of sleep can seriously ___ a student's concentration.
example.solution: **affect** — a verb is needed after 'can', meaning influence; effect is usually the noun.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One verb (call, look, put, turn, give) is shown with the particle missing, or the options are four verb + particle combinations.
pyqPatterns.approach: Say the meaning the sentence needs in plain words (cancel, investigate, tolerate, postpone, emit), then choose the particle that gives that meaning. Watch for 'look forward to', where to is a preposition and takes V-ing.

example.q: Because of the cyclone warning, the fair was put ___ till next month.
example.solution: **off** — put off = postpone; 'till next month' confirms the delay.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Time anchors (since, for, by the time, when, if, had) surround the blank; the options are one verb in different tenses or forms.
pyqPatterns.approach: Circle the anchor. since/for -> perfect; earlier of two past events -> had + V3; if (type 1) -> simple present; Had + subject + V3 -> would have + V3; enjoy/deny -> V-ing; decide/refuse -> to + V1. Check agreement last (neither of / the number of -> singular).

example.q: Had she left home earlier, she ___ the flight.
example.solution: **would have caught** — the inverted type-3 condition needs would have + V3.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The blank joins two clauses (although, because, yet) or a noun to a clause (who, whom, whose, which), or completes a hardly/no sooner frame.
pyqPatterns.approach: Name the relationship between the two sides (contrast, cause, result, time) and choose the connector with that meaning. Then check what follows: despite/because of take a noun, although/because take a clause. For pronouns: who = subject, whom = object or after a preposition, whose = possession.

example.q: The scientist to ___ the award was given belongs to Kerala.
example.solution: **whom** — a preposition needs the object form; 'to who' is ungrammatical.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two blanks, and every option is a comma-joined pair: correlatives (neither, nor), fixed idioms (safe, sound) or range pairs (from, to).
pyqPatterns.approach: Test each whole pair in place. Remove pairs with mismatched partners first (neither ... or, hardly ... than). Then use the visible verb: both ... and takes a plural verb, while neither/either ... nor/or agree with the nearer subject. Read to the full stop before choosing.

example.q: ___ the teachers ___ the principal was informed about the inspection.
example.solution: **Neither, nor** — the singular 'was' agrees with the nearer 'principal'; 'Both ... and' would need 'were'.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The sentence opens with Hardly had, Scarcely had or No sooner had, and the blank is the second partner (or the auxiliary 'had').
pyqPatterns.approach: No sooner -> than; hardly / scarcely -> when. The first clause is in the past perfect (had + V3) and the second in the simple past. 'Then' is always a decoy.

example.q: No sooner had the rain stopped ___ the children ran out to play.
example.solution: **than** — the only partner of no sooner; 'when' belongs to hardly and scarcely.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The manager managed to ___ a balance between the two demanding clients.
solvedExamples.solution: The fixed partnership is **strike a balance** (= find a middle position). *Knock/break/pull a balance* are not English partnerships — the options are ordinary verbs placed to test pairing memory, not meaning.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Recall the partnership, not the dictionary: balance → strike.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The villagers could no longer put ___ with the erratic power supply.
solvedExamples.solution: The sentence needs 'tolerate': **put up with**. *Put on* wears, *put off* postpones, *put in* installs — each particle builds a different verb. The cue 'could no longer' + a nuisance noun demands the tolerate-unit.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Name the action (tolerate) and match the unit: tolerate = put up with.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ the students ___ the teacher was aware of the change in schedule.
solvedExamples.solution: The verb *was* is singular. 'Both...and' demands a plural verb (*were*), and 'Neither, or' is not a pair. With *Either...or*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject — *the teacher* (singular) → **was**, exactly as the sentence reads. 'Not only, but' is incomplete without 'also'.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Verb agreement decides the pair: singular was after a two-part subject → Either...or (nearer subject singular).

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The two leaders held detailed ___ on the border dispute.
practice.solution: 'Held detailed ___ on a dispute' asks for the discussion partnership: **deliberations**. The other options share the -tion shape but belong to wrong topics — parties celebrate, patients take medication, sound reverberates.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The new taxation policy will have a far-reaching ___ on small traders.
practice.solution: After the article *a* the blank must be a noun, and the meaning is 'result': **effect**. *Affect* is the verb; *affection* is fondness; *effectiveness* needs no 'a far-reaching' frame and changes the meaning.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The company had to call ___ the proposed merger after the audit report.
practice.solution: Action = cancel: **call off**. *Call up* telephones, *call out* challenges/announces, *call for* demands — none survives the substitution test.
practice.shortcut: Substitute 'cancel' — the surviving particle is off.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The retired professor could not put ___ with the constant construction noise.
practice.solution: Tolerate = **put up with**, a three-word unit whose object follows ('with the noise'). *Put on/off/in/across* build other meanings — wear, postpone, install, communicate.
practice.shortcut: Nuisance + 'could not' → tolerate → put up with.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

By the time the firefighters arrived, the wooden shed ___ to ashes.
practice.solution: 'By the time + past event' makes the blank the earlier of two past actions → past perfect: **had burnt**. Present-perfect options clash with the past anchor, and 'was burning' describes a mid-process rather than the completed ruin.
practice.shortcut: By-the-time ladder: earlier event → had + participle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I look forward to ___ from you at the earliest.
practice.solution: 'Look forward to' is prepositional ('forward to it'), so the -ing form follows: **hearing**. The other options serve an infinitive or passive slot that this frame does not have.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ it rained heavily throughout the day, the final match was not ___.
practice.solution: The clauses contrast (rain vs the match happening) → concession: **Although** — this eliminates both 'Because' pairs. A match that is not played is **called off**; *called on* visits, *called up* telephones. Only the first pair completes both halves.
practice.shortcut: Anchor the connective (contrast → Although), then match the phrasal to the meaning.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Hardly had the chief guest taken his seat ___ the curtains rose.
practice.solution: 'Hardly had...' partners with **when**: 'Hardly had X happened when Y happened'. *Than* belongs exclusively to 'No sooner...than'.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The paediatrician ___ the mother to complete the full course of medicine.
practice.solution: The sentence needs a finite past verb after its subject: **advised**. *Advice* is a noun, *advices* is not standard English, *advising* cannot serve alone as the verb.
practice.shortcut: Frame first: subject + blank + object → finite verb → advised.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

All the ___ items — pens, registers and markers — were locked in the storeroom.
practice.solution: Pens, registers and markers are writing materials: **stationery**. *Stationary* means not moving — the items may be stationary too, but the apposition with the list pins the meaning to the writing-materials word.
practice.shortcut: Context picture: pens and registers → stationery.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The union leader ___ every worker trusts was re-elected without a contest.
practice.solution: Rephrase the clause: 'every worker trusts (him)' — object role, person → **whom**. *Whose* shows possession, *which* serves things, *what* does not introduce such relative clauses.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The Principal congratulated the debate team ___ winning the national championship.
practice.solution: The fixed partnership is **congratulate on**: 'congratulated the team on winning'. The -ing after the blank is exactly what this frame expects.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The auditorium was ___ small ___ accommodate the entire graduating batch.
practice.solution: Adjective + bare verb after the second blank → the *too + adj + to + base verb* structure: **too small to accommodate**. 'So, that' would need a full clause ('so small that it could not accommodate'), 'very' forms no pair, and 'too, for' needs a noun after 'for'.
practice.shortcut: Recognise the skeleton: too + adj + to + verb.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ the manager ___ his assistants were responsible for the filing error.
practice.solution: The verb *were* is plural, and 'Both...and' is the only listed pair that takes plural agreement. 'Either, or' would agree with the nearer subject (*assistants* — plural!) — but the pair 'Neither, or' is invalid English, and 'Not only, but' is incomplete without 'also'.
practice.shortcut: Verb agreement tiebreak: plural were with a full two-part subject → Both...and.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The minister gave a solemn ___ that the pending project would be cleared within a month.
practice.solution: A solemn statement meant to remove doubt is an **assurance** — the noun partner of *assure*. *Insurance* covers risk by policy, *endurance* is the power to bear hardship, *abundance* is plenty — none fits 'gave a solemn ___ that'.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The annual sports meet will ___ place in the second week of December.
practice.solution: Events **take place** — a fixed verb + noun chunk. 'Give place', 'make place' and 'hold place' are not used for an event happening.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The new trainee ___ several mistakes in his first report but corrected them quickly.
practice.solution: Mistakes are **made** (or committed). 'Did mistakes' is the commonest Indian-English slip; 'took' and 'gave' do not partner mistake at all.
practice.shortcut: make a mistake, never do a mistake.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Commuters were stuck for hours in ___ traffic on the highway.
practice.solution: Dense traffic is **heavy traffic**, the same partner as heavy rain. 'Strong', 'powerful' and 'weighty' are near-synonyms that refuse this noun.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The bus driver had a ___ escape when the truck swerved into his lane.
practice.solution: Escaping danger by very little is a **narrow escape**. 'Thin', 'slim' and 'tight' all mean small, but none is the fixed partner of escape.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Wear a jacket in the evening, or you may ___ a cold.
practice.solution: Illness is **caught**: catch a cold, catch a fever. 'Grab', 'hold' and 'seize' are literal verbs of taking and do not form the idiom.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

By the time the guests left, the children were ___ asleep on the sofa.
practice.solution: Deep sleep is **fast asleep** — here fast means firmly, not speedily. 'Quick', 'rapid' and 'swift' only carry the speed sense, so none partners asleep.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

It is ___ and parcel of a journalist's job to verify every claim.
practice.solution: The frozen expression is **part and parcel**, meaning an essential part. Its words cannot be swapped, so 'piece', 'bit' and 'section' break the idiom.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The defence lawyer's argument did not ___ water, and the appeal was dismissed.
practice.solution: An argument that is sound **holds water**. The idiom is frozen: 'keep water', 'retain water' and 'bear water' describe containers, not reasoning. The dismissed appeal confirms the argument was weak.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

After a long debate, the committee finally ___ a conclusion.
practice.solution: One **reaches a conclusion** directly. 'Arrived' needs at (arrived at a conclusion) and 'came' needs to (came to a conclusion); neither takes the noun straight after it. 'Got a conclusion' is not idiomatic.
practice.shortcut: reach a conclusion / arrive AT / come TO.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The two companies ___ a deal worth several crores late last night.
practice.solution: Agreements are **struck**: strike a deal, strike a balance, strike a bargain. 'Beat', 'knocked' and 'smashed' are hitting verbs used literally and do not form the business chunk.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The opposition ___ the minister's resignation after the scam came to light.
practice.solution: The sense needed is demanded: **called for** the resignation. 'Called off' means cancelled, 'called on' means visited or urged a person, and 'called up' means telephoned.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The bank decided to call ___ the loan when the borrower missed three instalments.
practice.solution: To demand repayment of a loan is to **call it in**. 'Call off' would cancel the loan, which a bank would not do to a defaulter; 'call on' and 'call up' do not take a loan as object.
practice.shortcut: call in a loan = demand it back.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

After the inquiry, the rumour ___ to be completely false.
practice.solution: The sense is 'proved to be': **turned out** to be false. 'Turned up' means appeared, 'turned down' means rejected, 'turned over' means handed over or flipped.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Grandmother looks ___ the baby while the parents are at work.
practice.solution: Caring for someone is **looking after** them. 'Look into' means investigate, 'look for' means search, 'look up' means find in a book or visit.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Young cricketers look ___ to the captain as their role model.
practice.solution: To admire is to **look up to** someone, and the phrase 'as their role model' confirms admiration. 'Look forward to' means anticipate, 'look down' suggests contempt, and 'look back to' means recall the past.
practice.shortcut: look up to = admire; look down on = despise.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

They are looking forward ___ their grandparents during the vacation.
practice.solution: In **look forward to**, 'to' is a preposition, so a gerund follows: **to meeting**. 'To meet' treats it as an infinitive — the classic trap. 'For meeting' uses the wrong particle, and bare 'meeting' drops the required to.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Because of the cyclone warning, the fair was put ___ till next month.
practice.solution: Postponed = **put off**, and 'till next month' confirms a delay. 'Put up' means house or raise, 'put down' means suppress, 'put across' means communicate.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The speaker failed to put ___ his ideas clearly to the audience.
practice.solution: Communicating ideas to listeners is **putting them across**. 'Put off' would postpone them, 'put up with' means tolerate, and 'put in' means insert or contribute.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The workers refused to ___ in to the management's pressure.
practice.solution: Surrender is **give in to**. 'Turn in' means hand over or go to bed, 'carry in' is literal, and 'take in' means absorb or deceive — none fits 'to the pressure'.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The old tanker ___ off thick black smoke as it climbed the ghat road.
practice.solution: To emit is to **give off**: gave off smoke, gave off a smell. 'Took off' means left the ground, 'called off' means cancelled, 'set off' means started a journey or triggered.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

She ___ in Pune since 2020.
practice.solution: 'Since 2020' ties a past start to the present, so the perfect is required: **has been living**. The simple present, present continuous and simple past cannot take a since-point.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

We ___ each other since our school days.
practice.solution: 'Since' needs the perfect, and 'know' is a stative verb that does not take a continuous form. That leaves **have known**. 'Are knowing' and 'had been knowing' break the stative rule, and 'know' ignores since.
practice.shortcut: Stative verb + since -> present perfect simple.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

When we reached the platform, the train ___.
practice.solution: Two past events: the train left first and we reached later. The earlier one takes the past perfect: **had already left**. 'Has already left' clashes with the past 'reached'.
practice.shortcut: Earlier of two past events -> had + V3.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

No sooner ___ the principal entered the hall than the students stood up.
practice.solution: The frame is 'No sooner had + subject + V3 ... than + simple past': **had** entered. 'Did' would need the base form 'enter', 'has' clashes with 'stood', and 'was entered' is a wrong passive.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

If it ___ tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
practice.solution: Type-1 conditional: the if-clause takes the simple present (**rains**) and the main clause takes will. 'Will' never enters the if-clause; 'rained' and 'would rain' belong to type 2.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Had she left home earlier, she ___ the flight.
practice.solution: The inverted 'Had she left' is a type-3 (unreal past) condition, so the result takes **would have caught**. 'Would catch' is type 2, 'will catch' is type 1, and 'had caught' has no would.
practice.shortcut: Had + subject + V3 ... would have + V3.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The children enjoy ___ in the rain.
practice.solution: 'Enjoy' is followed by a gerund: enjoy **playing**. 'Enjoy to play' is the common slip; 'play' and 'to playing' are not possible after enjoy.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The committee decided ___ the event to December.
practice.solution: 'Decide' takes the infinitive: decided **to postpone**. 'Decided postponing' uses the gerund wrongly; the bare verb and 'to postponing' are ungrammatical here.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Neither of the two answers ___ correct.
practice.solution: 'Neither of + plural noun' takes a singular verb because neither (not one) is the head. So **is**. 'Are', 'were' and 'have been' agree with 'answers', the trap noun.
practice.shortcut: neither of / each of -> singular verb.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The number of applicants for the post ___ increased sharply this year.
practice.solution: 'The number of' is singular (one number), so **has** increased. 'A number of' would be plural — that is the distinction being tested. 'Are increased' and 'were increased' are wrong passives with the wrong number.
practice.shortcut: THE number -> singular; A number -> plural.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

No sooner had the rain stopped ___ the children ran out to play.
practice.solution: 'No sooner' pairs only with **than**. 'When' belongs to hardly or scarcely, 'then' is a time adverb, and 'that' is not a correlative.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The patient had scarcely reached the hospital ___ he lost consciousness.
practice.solution: 'Scarcely' (like hardly) pairs with **when**. 'Than' is the partner of no sooner, the mix-up the question is testing; 'then' and 'so' do not complete the frame.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

This is the house ___ roof was damaged in the storm.
